deliverables.text: A complete factorization of the original formula, O(n), from Appendix A: find the greatest common factor of its coefficients using prime factorization -- show a factor tree or repeated division for each coefficient, label every prime factor you find, and note any place an intermediate number turns out to be composite and needs further breaking down -- then write O(n) as (greatest common factor) x (remaining expression).

The same complete factorization for the AI-rewritten formula, R(n), from Appendix A: find the greatest common factor of ITS coefficients using prime factorization, following the same process as D1, and write R(n) in fully factored form.

A sample-test table: evaluate O(n) and R(n) at all three batch sizes in Appendix B -- the two batches QA already tested, and the one representative larger batch QA has not tested -- showing every calculation, and state whether the two formulas still agree at each batch size, in dollars and as a percent.

A written proof verdict: using ONLY the fully factored forms from D1 and D2 (not D3's plugged-in numbers), determine whether O(n) and R(n) are the same expression for every possible batch size, or only coincidentally equal at the two batch sizes QA happened to test. Name the specific structural feature the factored form reveals -- visible in the factored forms but invisible in D3's matching outputs -- that answers the question.

A cost comparison table: using Appendix C's verification-labor figures and Appendix D's risk-exposure figures, calculate in dollars the cost of Option A (the expected cost of approving now, given the stated risk of an undetected error) versus Option B (the cost of paying for a full factoring verification today), and state which option is cheaper on paper, in dollars and as a percent.

A one-paragraph recommendation memo to Priya's engineering director: using BOTH D4's proof result and D5's cost comparison, state which option you recommend and defend it -- including whether D4's result changes how much you trust the risk figure used in D5.

appendices.title: Verification Cost and the Deployment Calendar

balance.argument_a: The Regression Pass shipped on the strength of a real two-batch match (O and R both give $1,488 at n=4 and $6,600 at n=10 -- Appendix B), clears before the 6-week deployment freeze (MA5/MA6), and costs nothing directly today. Weighed only against Appendix D's stated pre-proof risk figures (3.4% chance of an undetected defect [grounded by S2] x $25,000 cost if one reaches production = $850.00 expected cost, MA8/MA9), Option A's expected cost is not wildly worse than Option B's $783.04 verification cost -- the two are only 7.88% apart on the numbers as stated before anyone does the proof, and MA9 (the cost-of-error figure) is itself the case's single most load-bearing, flippable dial (see sensitivity_disclosure): at -50%, A's expected cost drops below B's, flipping the pre-proof recommendation entirely.
balance.argument_b: The Full Factor costs a fixed $783.04 (2 engineers x 8 hours x $48.94/hr [S1], MA7) and buys a proof, not a probability. D1/D2's factoring shows O(n)=12n(4n+15) has n as a factor of every term (so a zero-item batch sweeps exactly $0, as it must) while R(n)=6(9n^2+16n+40) never does (it sweeps $240 even at n=0) -- meaning the two formulas are structurally different and can only coincidentally agree at the two specific batch sizes (n=4, n=10) that QA happened to test. Once D4's proof exists, Appendix D's 3.4% probability is revealed as understating the real risk for any batch outside {4, 10}: at n=25, O and R already diverge by $1,890 (5.5%); at a real production batch of n=40, they diverge by $6,480 (7.7%) every single night. B's $783.04 is cheap next to a recurring, provable error of that size.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |cost_A - cost_B| / max(cost_A, cost_B), where cost_B (The Full Factor) = engineers x hours_per_engineer x hourly_wage = 2 x 8 x $48.94 = $783.04 (MA7, [S1]), and cost_A (The Regression Pass) = p_defect x cost_of_undetected_error = 0.034 x $25,000 = $850.00 (MA8, MA9). margin = |850.00-783.04|/850.00 = 7.88%, within the case's 5-10% target band and SPEC §2's 20% cap. This is the pre-proof margin only -- D4's proof (see argument_b) separately shows the formulas are not equivalent outside n={4,10}, which is not itself expressed as a margin_pct but is the case's real pedagogical payload. Full arithmetic: sensitivity_model.py.

No real company's actual formula is used or implied.

Grounded in real, general evidence (S2: CodeRabbit's analysis of 470 real pull requests found AI-authored code carries 1.4-1.7x more critical/major defects than human-written code, logic/correctness issues 75% more common) that the underlying risk is real and material; 3.4% is a modest, non-zero residual-risk figure chosen for a change that has already cleared some testing, not a direct read-off of S2's aggregate statistic.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Cost if an undetected reconciliation-sweep error reaches production
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a cost specific to a systemic formula-level reconciliation error at a private financial-infrastructure company. General industry commentary on reconciliation-exception handling documents routine per-exception investigation costs around $9-$22; a systemic, formula-level error recurring every affected night and requiring multi-batch investigation plus compliance/audit escalation is categorically more severe, so $25,000 is set well above that routine range as a disclosed scenario value, not derived arithmetically from it.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tier 2 P5 found a -50% flex ($12,500) drops Option A's expected cost to $425.00, flipping D5's pre-proof recommendation to The Regression Pass. This is exactly why D6 requires reconciling D5 against D4's proof rather than trusting D5 alone -- see sensitivity_disclosure.

sensitivity_note: T3 tier: the case's D5 cost comparison rests on two stated Modeling Assumptions (MA8 the defect probability, MA9 the cost-of-error) that no public source publishes for this scenario -- MA9 is the dilemma-flipping dial on D5's pre-proof metric (see modeling_assumptions[MA9].sensitivity and sensitivity_disclosure below). D4's proof result (whether the factored forms share a common factor of n) is a fixed structural fact of MA1/MA2, not a flexed assumption.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: The dollar cost of investigating and correcting a systemic, undetected reconciliation-formula error at a specific fictional company is a forecast/estimate of a rare, severe event -- not a measurable present fact, and no public source publishes it. Tier 2 P5 found -50% flex ($12,500) drops Option A's expected cost to $425.00, below Option B's fixed $783.04 -- flipping D5's pre-proof recommendation from The Full Factor to The Regression Pass. (+50%, $37,500, raises Option A to $1,275.00 and does not flip the base B-favoring result.) Consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA9].

The probability that this specific, already-partially-tested AI-rewritten formula still contains an undetected defect is an estimate, not a measurable fact -- grounded qualitatively by real evidence (S2) that AI-generated code carries elevated defect rates, but the exact residual probability for this scenario is inherently unpublishable. Tier 2 P5 found -50% flex (1.7%) drops Option A's expected cost to $425.00, below Option B's $783.04 -- flipping the pre-proof recommendation to The Regression Pass, the same direction and for the same underlying reason as cost_of_error (both are multiplicative factors of the same cost_A product). (+50%, 5.1%, raises Option A to $1,275.00 and does not flip the base result.) Consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA8].

How many hours a full symbolic factoring verification actually takes is an internal staffing estimate, not a measurable fact. Tier 2 P5 found +50% flex (12 hours) raises Option B's cost to $1,174.56, above Option A's base $850.00 -- flipping the pre-proof recommendation to The Regression Pass. This is the case's one flip point in the OPPOSITE direction from cost_of_error/p_defect (it flips by making verification more expensive, not by making the risk look cheaper). (-50%, 4 hours, lowers Option B to $391.52 and does not flip the base result.) Consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA7].
